claims.claim: pike, muskellunge, tiger muskellunge 150–225 mm on fathead minnow / gizzard shad / bluegill at optimal size (25–43 % of predator length): 0.67 / 0.78 / 0.14 captures per strike; 700-L tank, 15 prey, 18–23 °C, 1-h trials
claims.location: p. 142 (PDF p. 2), abstract; p. 143 (PDF p. 3), Methods; p. 144–145 (PDF pp. 4–5), Results and Fig. 1
claims.quote: mean captures per strike were higher for fathead minnow (0.67) and gizzard shad (0.78)
claims.conditions: 225 one-hour trials in a 700-L (260 × 53 × 60 cm) tank without cover, 18–23 °C; hatchery esocids 150–225 mm TL, conditioned to the prey ≥ 2 weeks and starved 24 h; naive single-species prey groups of 15; prey 25–30 % (bluegill), 37–43 % (fathead), 30–36 % (shad) of predator length; means of 5 individuals per taxon, 3–7 replicates each; the three esocids did not differ
claims.note: the 25–43 % "optimal" sizes are not W&S's own: they come from Gillen et al. 1981 (lab; minimal handling time per unit dry weight) and Carline et al. 1986 (field, shad)

claims.claim: esocids catch deep-bodied, spiny sunfish on about one strike in seven
claims.conditions: bluegill at 25–30 % of predator length, laboratory tank without cover

claims.paper: §4.5 (capture success); src/w3/fish3.js:983–984 (CS3: soft-rayed 0.7 to an esocid)

claims.note: (0.67 + 0.78)/2 = 0.725. The model extends it to killifish, dace, alewife, fallfish and sucker, which were not tested

claims.claim: an esocid lands 0.12 of strikes on sunfish (after Wahl & Stein 1988)

claims.note: 0.12 is not printed; it lies between the pike's ~0.10 and the pooled 0.14. Say "0.14 on bluegill (pike alone ~0.10)" or state that 0.12 is a project choice

claims.paper: src/w3/fish3.js:138 (PREY_OPT / PREY_PREF: preference for prey of an optimal length)
claims.claim: optimal prey 25–43 % of a predator's length (Wahl & Stein 1988)
claims.source_value: 25–43 % are the prey sizes W&S chose as optimal from Gillen et al. 1981 and Carline et al. 1986; "optimal" means minimal handling time per unit prey dry weight, not an observed preference
claims.quote: Optimal sizes of prey were based on laboratory experiments (Gillen et al. 1981)
claims.note: cite Gillen et al. 1981 (via Wahl & Stein 1988), and note the definition: W&S give "minimal ratio of esocid handling time per unit of dry weight of prey" (p. 142). The model uses it as a choice preference, which the source did not measure

claims.paper: src/w3/fish3.js:102 (STRIKE2: capture success by predator kind)
claims.claim: capture success depends on the prey species and the predator's kind (CS3, after Wahl & Stein 1988 for esocids)
claims.quote: to make five times as many strikes to capture them
claims.conditions: esocids on bluegill vs fathead/shad; the three esocid taxa did not differ in capture ability

claims.claim: esocids caught and preferred fathead minnows over bluegill
claims.source_value: caught: yes (0.67 vs 0.14 per strike). Preferred: not tested for fathead vs bluegill (single-species trials; esocids attacked MORE bluegills, 5.8 vs 3.2 per trial). The field preference measured was gizzard shad over bluegill (Chesson's α 0.91–1.00, Kokosing Reservoir)
claims.location: p. 144 (PDF p. 4); p. 146 (PDF p. 6); p. 149 (PDF p. 9), Table 5
claims.quote: esocids strongly preferred gizzard shad and not bluegills (Table 5)
claims.note: say "caught fathead minnows far more readily than bluegill and preferred gizzard shad over bluegill in the field"; the minnow preference is others' work cited in W&S's discussion (Beyerle & Williams 1968; Mauck & Coble 1971; Coble 1973; Weithman & Anderson 1977)

notes: Laboratory values hold. Corrections are in the model's use: the sunfish value 0.12 is not printed (0.14 pooled, ~0.10 for pike alone); the bullhead 0.1 is not from this study; the shad were at 30–36 % of predator length, not 37–43 %; the 25–43 % 'optimal' sizes come from Gillen et al. 1981 and Carline et al. 1986 and are handling-cost optima, not a measured preference. Other useful values: handling times longest for bluegill; esocids attacked 5.8 bluegills, 3.2 fatheads and 1.4 shad per hour but consumed 0.5, 1.9 and 1.0; esocids captured bluegill midbody on only 40 % of captures (vs 67 % fathead, 72 % shad; Table 2, page image); in September–October empty stomachs were 72–95 % in the bluegill-only pond vs 22–72 % with shad (Table 4, page image); survival collapsed in the bluegill-only pond. No cover in the tanks (the authors argue the results extend to cover, citing Savino & Stein and Mauck & Coble).
